requirements.note: Grid of all 600 tiles, three per row edge to edge with hairline gaps, HSL squares with centred emoji, newest first; header reads '600 tiles · Newest first'.
Filter button in the nav bar opens a native menu with All Boards plus the ten boards and a checkmark on the current one; the grid and count update (Coast: 64 tiles). Liked has its own filter.

Push to a full-width large tile with the title in the nav bar, plus title, board and 'Added <date>'. Horizontal swipes move to the next or previous tile within the current filter ('2 of 64'). Prev/next buttons are also provided.
Like/Liked toggle button in the large view. The Liked tab shows the same grid with heart badges and updates immediately when a tile is unliked from it.

Select turns the title into 'N Selected' with Select All and Cancel, check circles on tiles, and a Like/Delete bar. Bulk like works. Bulk delete asks for confirmation in a system alert and removes the tiles (600→598).
After relaunch the likes (Liked count 66) and deletions (598) were kept.

tells: The nav title is a small inline 'Moodboard' with no large title, and it is left-aligned on Library but centred on Liked, so the two tabs disagree.
In the large view the Like button's heart and text are plain black/white rather than tinted, and the filled 'Liked' heart is black instead of red or the accent colour.
At the largest text size the emoji in the large view grows with Dynamic Type until it nearly fills the tile and looks soft and upscaled.
At the largest text size the select-mode Like/Delete bar takes up nearly half the screen, leaving about two rows of grid visible.
The select-mode action bar is a custom button strip floating above the tab bar, not a system bottom toolbar.
A.scroll: Slow drags, hard flings to the end and back, and the overscroll bounce all feel native, with no blank or popping tiles; scroll position is kept after visiting a tile and coming back.

requirements.note: Grid of all 600 tiles, three per row with 6pt margins and rounded corners, newest first, under a 'Find your next inspiration.' hero header.
An 'All boards' pill button opens a native menu with All boards plus the ten boards and a checkmark; the grid and count update (Coast: 64 tiles).
Pushes a large rounded tile in a horizontally paging collection with prev/next arrows, 'n of N', serif title, board chip and 'Added <date>'. Swipes move to neighbouring tiles.
A large accent Like/Liked button pinned at the bottom. The Liked tab shows the same grid with heart badges and drops a tile when it is unliked there.
Select shows 'N selected' with Select all and Done, check circles plus a selection outline, and a Like/Delete bar. Bulk like works, and bulk delete confirms then removes the tiles (600→598).
After relaunch the likes (Liked 65) and deletions (598) were kept.

bugs: The delete confirmation popover is anchored near the top of the screen with its arrow pointing at the 'All boards' filter, not at the Delete button that was tapped.
tells: A marketing-style hero ('Find your next inspiration.' / 'Keep what moves you.' in a large serif, with a tagline) above the grid looks like a web landing page, not an iOS list screen.
The glass circle at the left of the nav bar holds a decorative grid or heart image that looks like a button but does nothing.
The large view's nav title is the generic 'A closer look' instead of the tile's name, and the view adds filler copy ('Something to spark an idea.').
At the largest text size the filter pill's leading icon and chevron and the detail view's arrow buttons stay tiny next to huge text, and the hero header disappears.
The tile count is split into two right-aligned lines ('600 tiles' / 'Newest first') in an unusual header layout.
The select-mode action bar is a custom floating Like/Delete pair rather than a system bottom toolbar.
B.scroll: Slow drags, flings to the end and back, and the overscroll bounce all feel native, with no blank or popping tiles; scroll position is kept after visiting a tile and coming back, and there is a footer line at the end.

why: Both apps meet all six requirements, including persistence, and both scroll smoothly. A looks like a Photos-style native app with a standard confirmation alert. B is more decorated, with a web-like serif hero, a decorative nav button that does nothing, a generic detail title and a delete popover anchored to the wrong control. A's flaws are smaller: an untinted like heart, no large title, and an oversized emoji at the largest text size.
